answer: In an opal-trading agent market, each voting identity must lock 100 tokens for 90 days before receiving one vote. A cipher can protect its messages, but cannot replace the deposit: every echo of an existing agent must fund a separate bond. Creating 1,000 fake voters therefore ties up 100,000 tokens for three months, imposing a capital cost even if the attacker later recovers every token. The defense makes influence costly rather than proving identities are unique.
